intro: Milestones in the debate, from the first synopsis to the present. Dates are those of the first publication of the work named. Where an idea was first put forward earlier, the entry says so.

items.what: Publishes the first synopsis: Matthew, Mark and Luke in parallel columns, laid out for comparison rather than harmonised. It made the agreements in order visible for the first time.
His *Neue Hypothese* (written 1778, published posthumously) derives the Gospels from a lost Aramaic “Urgospel”. This was the first of several lost-gospel theories.

*Commentatio* (1789–90): Mark abbreviated and combined Matthew and Luke, turning to Luke whenever he left Matthew's order. Griesbach had announced the thesis in 1783, and Henry Owen had suggested the same order in 1764. G. C. Storr had argued in 1786 for the reverse: Mark first, then Luke, then Matthew using both. Griesbach's view held wide acceptance in Germany until about 1860.

Schleiermacher (1832) takes Papias's statement that Matthew compiled the λόγια (“oracles”) to mean a collection of Jesus' sayings, the seed of the sayings-source idea. Lachmann (1835) argues from the order of the narratives that Mark best preserves the common sequence.

items.who: C. H. Weisse; C. G. Wilke
items.what: In the same year, Weisse proposes that Matthew and Luke used Mark and a sayings source, the first form of the Two-Source hypothesis (Kloppenborg calls it a forerunner). Wilke proposes Mark first, with Matthew using Luke, the forerunner of Matthean Posteriority.

*Die synoptischen Evangelien* is often credited with establishing the Two-Source hypothesis. It uses a proto-Mark (A) and a sayings source (Λ); Holtzmann dropped the proto-Mark in 1886. Around 1880, with E. Simons, he allowed that Luke also made subsidiary use of Matthew.
From Weiss onwards the sayings source, earlier called “the λόγια”, is known as Q (*Quelle*, “source”).

Wernle's monograph argues that Matthew and Luke used Mark itself, so Q is more or less the double tradition. Hawkins's *Horae Synopticae* supplies the word statistics that British scholarship relied on, and explains many minor agreements as independent editing of a Mark almost identical with ours.
*Oxford Studies in the Synoptic Problem*, from the Oxford seminar Sanday led from 1894. It includes Streeter on Mark's knowledge of Q.
*The Four Gospels* sets out the classic British form: Mark, Q, M and L, plus Proto-Luke. It explains the minor agreements chiefly as independent editing and textual assimilation.

A Coptic Gospel of Thomas is found: a sayings gospel without a passion narrative. Q theorists cite it as evidence that collections of sayings existed, which answers Farrer's objection that nothing like Q is attested.
*The Originality of St Matthew* names the “Lachmann fallacy”: the agreements in order show only that Mark is the middle term between Matthew and Luke, not that Mark was first.
“On Dispensing with Q”: if Luke could have read Matthew, the question Q answers never arises. It drew little response at first.

items.who: W. R. Farmer; J. M. Robinson
items.what: Farmer's *The Synoptic Problem* reopens the question and revives Griesbach. In the same year Robinson's essay “LOGOI SOPHON” (ET 1971) assigns Q to the genre of sayings of the wise.
*Midrash and Lection in Matthew*, followed by *Luke: A New Paradigm* (1989), makes the Farrer hypothesis a sustained programme. In 1974 Neirynck also publishes his catalogue of the minor agreements.

At the Jerusalem symposium Boismard, Farmer and Neirynck present competing hypotheses side by side, and the Griesbach team sets out its statement of the Two-Gospel hypothesis. In the same year Tuckett shows that the alternating support for Mark's order is also compatible with the Two-Source hypothesis. The symposium papers appeared as *The Interrelations of the Gospels* (ed. D. L. Dungan, BETL 95, 1990).
*The Formation of Q* argues that Q was a Greek document composed in layers. Studies of Q as a gospel with its own theology and community follow.

*The Critical Edition of Q* (eds. J. M. Robinson, P. Hoffmann and J. S. Kloppenborg) prints a reconstructed text with graded degrees of certainty. It is the product of IQP work sessions whose reports appeared in *JBL* from 1990.
*The Case Against Q* restates the Farrer case without Goulder's lectionary theory and without denying Luke other sources. *Questioning Q* (eds. Goodacre and N. Perrin, 2004) gathers further essays.
*New Studies in the Synoptic Problem* (eds. P. Foster, A. Gregory, J. S. Kloppenborg and J. Verheyden, BETL 239), from the April 2008 Oxford conference honouring C. M. Tuckett.

*Marcan Priority without Q* (LNTS 455) is the first multi-author volume on the Farrer hypothesis. MacEwen's *Matthean Posteriority* (LNTS 501) is the first monograph on Matthew's use of Luke, and Garrow's *NTS* articles follow in 2016.

*The Synoptic Problem: Four Views*: Evans (Two-Source), Goodacre (Farrer), Peabody (Two-Gospel) and Riesner (orality and memory). In the same year Kirk's *Q in Matthew* gives a media-and-memory defence of Q.

*Gospel Interpretation and the Q-Hypothesis* (LNTS 573), from the international conference at Roskilde, Denmark, in June 2015 (organised by M. Müller, S. Nordgaard and H. Omerzu). Q's defenders, sceptics and the undecided appear in one volume, including the Tuckett–Watson exchange and Goodacre on the Mark–Q overlaps.

*Relating the Gospels* and *Solving the Synoptic Puzzle*: the fullest Farrer case since 2002, built on memory and ancient imitation. Klinghardt's *The Oldest Gospel* (English edition) puts Marcion's Gospel in the place of Q.

*The Synoptic Problem 2022* (BiTS 44) gathers papers for a Loyola Chicago conference planned for 2020 and cancelled because of Covid-19; its publisher describes it as the first such volume in which Matthean Posteriority is prominently represented. *The Oxford Handbook of the Synoptic Gospels* (ed. S. P. Ahearne-Kroll) opens with Kloppenborg's survey of the problem.

Barker's *Writing and Rewriting the Gospels* (Mark, Matthew, Luke, then John, with no Q) and Goodacre's *The Fourth Synoptic Gospel* carry the Farrer logic over to John. Tuckett's *NovT* article answers Matthean Posteriority.
